title: The Judge's Impartiality and the Conscience
english: "His steps will not be made to slip." (Prov 4:26). For the law of God is in the heart of the righteous; he meditates on wisdom and his steps are not made to slip, which are "the walking powers of the soul." Such a thing also the saying of Proverbs means, "the judgments of the thoughts of the righteous" (Prov 20:27). And when such thoughts exist, the word follows to be like this: "for the good man brings forth good out of the good treasure of the heart" (Luke 6:45). Whether you speak not in the presence of the Lord, and speak deceit toward him, or whether you shrink back? From their own conscience he begins to teach them by reproof, that whatever they bring forth, seeing God, they speak; but he also announces to them the deceit as being brought forth in his presence for the sake of correction, so that they might cease from such a disposition, since they have the Lord watching over them. And therefore he prevents their audacity, because just as they shrank back from a man, hiding deceit and speaking against him, [so they do to God].

The words are useful against those who lie and use deceit, concerning which also David says: "of those speaking peace with their neighbors, but evil in their hearts" (Ps 55:21). But you yourselves become judges. It is well, if it searches you out. If anyone says: "How is it that he just said 'you are unjust doctors' (Matt 23:27) and 'whether you speak not in the presence of the Lord, and speak deceit toward him'" and now says: "but you yourselves become judges"? To this it must be said: that each of those sinning, being enticed by pleasure, does not perceive the eye of the God who watches. But if a righteous and wise man, or even another such, is called, the conscience of the sinner leads him to the realization that God sees the inward thoughts of each, striking him into perception. This is therefore what the saint does, saying: "but you yourselves become judges. It is well, if it searches you out." For those being conscious of a slip do not wish to be searched out even by a righteous man, how much less by God; for of the saints it is such, according to David saying: "refine my reins and my heart" (Ps 51:10). For if, doing all things, you are placed before him, nothing less will convict you. Even if the...

“Having done all things that must be done, you shall be added to him”—instead of “you shall make yourselves his own”—“you shall again be subject to reproof through ignorances.” This indeed the blessed apostle was saying: “I do not consider myself my own conscience, but not in this have I been justified” (cf. 1 Cor 4:4). For it enters into me to overlook something of the ignorances, and I have not been justified because of that. And as far as I think I have no conscience against myself, I think I am without responsibility. But it is not my judgment that shows me having been justified, but the judgment of God.

The blessed David also confirms this, saying: “Who will understand trespasses? From my secret parts cleanse me” (Ps 51:2). For in truth, someone recognizes sins, but trespasses, which in a certain way are unintentional, someone hardly understands. “And if therefore,” he says, “you do all things toward purity, from the unintentional things, as from God judging, you shall have the reproof.” Through which also the Lord said to his own disciples: “When you have done all things, say: we are unprofitable slaves, what we ought to do, we have done” (Luke 17:10).

And if even in secret you should admire faces, whether not his agitation will trouble you, and fear will fall upon you from him? The best judge of matters is the examiner; he does not look toward the faces of those being judged. For if those being judged were rich or rulers or others possessing superior value, he does not look toward their face, but toward the actions, which he judges. This also is carried forward in the Catholic Epistle: “admiring faces for the sake of advantage” (Jas 2:9), and it is clear that the flatterers are justifying the ungodly because of gifts and removing the justice of the just. But God, standing as protector, does not will thus, but lays down law: “according to the great and the small you will judge, you will not receive a face,” clearly of the rich, and “you will not have mercy on the poor in judgment” (Deut 10:17). And it is said elsewhere: “justly let the just pursue the just.”

For it is not necessary to add to the rich, nor should the poor, pitying his need, overlook the just. And it becomes the work of a righteous judge, just as it is handed down in the history concerning David, so that after the judgments and outcomes of matters, if it should happen that the poor is there, or one who has ignored the just, or one acting unjustly, the rich man is exhorted so that he might show philanthropy toward him. And the righteousness of the judge will be more ready for this.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Purpose of Sin's Ashes and the Body's Nature
english: Accepting. Thus indeed it is said concerning David: 'doing judgment and justice' (Ps 72:2). ... Job ... 'if you also marvel at faces in secret' (Job 27:19); for every bribetaker does not accept the things of those providing from the visible, but in secret, often also in a disguised manner, according to that, he wishes to come together. And he brings fear, saying that if someone dares to hide the thing of partiality by craft, but God, being angry through the onslaught against the sinners, will shake them, instead of 'he will let the passion be provided to them.'

He says the onslaught with the impulse of passion is like the movement of the swirling waters according to the dawnings, so that what he says briefly is such: 'do you bring his movement, if he is indignant?' Similar to this is what is brought in Zechariah, said to the sinners: 'the Lord shall go in the whirlwind of his wrath' (Zech 9:4). And the whirlwind of wrath signifies the anger because of their sins, for he himself is ... The 'shall go' might perhaps be similar to that said in Genesis concerning Adam, that he heard God walking just as he was sinning (Gen 3:8); through this he receives a sensation of the departure of God because he no longer has anything luminous in himself. For those lengthening themselves from God hear: 'the Lord is far from the ungodly' (Ps 144:5), not in place of this being said, but in distancing the one being good and the one being bad from Him. And these things are because of the 'shall go in the whirlwind.'

Let us return to the beginning, to those 'marveling at faces in secret,' whom also the anger of God according to a whirlwind will shake, as it was given; and upon them also fear falls from God, and this is for benefit, so that they may know that a threat is brought against them as sinners. And of this fear, which I say according to the threat, is another by which it is said: 'the fear of the Lord surpassed all' (Ps 112:7), which is primarily reverence. For there is no other fear of God or heightened respect, through which those having it become lacking; 'for there is no deficiency to those fearing him' (Ps 115:11). But the passive fear follows the sinners. For another of this kind is said to be sent upon sinners for punishment; observe...

Otherwise, it signifies nothing else through the name of fear or the avoidance of wrath. This is not a passion of God; for it is said, 'I sent away the wrath' (Ps 106:42/implied); a passion is not sent away. But your boasting shall pass away like ashes. The word shows the state after the wrath of those sinning, being brought to nothing in the revelation occurring through the wrath, the conceit of those judging secretly being consumed.

Since ashes signify worthlessness, it is to be learned from one of the twelve prophets saying, 'And you shall trample down the lawless and they shall be as ashes under your feet' (cf. Zephaniah/Prophetic imagery). For ashes are something burning that has lost its own power. Indeed, a threat regarding burning is brought in Deuteronomy, as through the fruits being hindered because the land has lost its own power. And it is for some benefit that sins are burned up; just as thorns and thistles, being burned, do not bring a little harm, so also the sins—even if they are burned according to what is said, 'the lawlessness shall be burned like fire and shall be consumed by fire like dry stubble' (Matt 13:40)—they no longer defile the soul, but are called out toward repentance according to what is said in the Gospel: 'If the powers that happened in you had occurred in Tyre and Sidon, long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes, they would have repented' (Matt 11:21).

For if anyone receives in his mind the salvation-fire, about which the Savior said, 'I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I want, if it is already kindled' (Luke 12:49), he burns up the former sins; and sitting, instead of 'having ceased from sinning,' he is turned toward repentance, choosing a somewhat severe and rigorous life. But the body is clay. Man is composed of soul and body. And there is a time when the body is led away as a slave by the soul and, in a certain way, is no longer being treated as clay, but being a servant to the soul along with reason and with the mind acting.

But when someone cares for nothing of his salvation, his soul, turning toward wickedness and serving the flesh, doing such things as do not differ from an irrational animal, he shows that his body is clay, as nothing helping from the soul's movements. For the body is something distinct from the soul, as the Savior himself taught, saying:
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Metaphor of Teeth and the Soul
english: “Do not fear those who kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul.” Since they are able to kill the body of a man, but not the soul, it is clear that the same essence is not of soul and body. Therefore, when the soul is hindered from its own and natural impulses, then the man appears as a body of clay, not because the soul is changing into a body, but because its actions are no longer heavenly, but bodily; just as Paul calls “those walking according to the flesh” (1 Cor 3:3) and “according to man” men, saying they have human qualities and not divine energy.

For it is said by the blessed Paul to all those who have devoted themselves to the bodily and because of this are being human in mind: “For where is strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to man?” (1 Cor 3:3). But when “walking upon the earth they have their citizenship in heaven” (Phil 3:20) and “bear the image of the heavenly” (2 Cor 4:4), they are not a body of clay. “You have made me deaf, so that I may speak and rest my spirit.” He says this, urging them to recognize those coming against them, shifting the cause to the saying “and rest my spirit,” instructing that if they might chance to be corrected from the state of being divided, his spirit—which he had rightfully been angry against their iniquity, not passionably, but as the law is laid down to be angry against sinners—would rest.

And the name of deafness signifies silence, as in “I was deaf and I did not open my mouth, because you are the one who made me” (Ps 31:9). For he says that not speaking is deafness. And again: “When the sinner stood against me, I was deaf and I was humbled, and he was silent from good things.” For when the sinner, who is the devil, having persuaded the soul to sin before it, reproaching it as “an enemy existing and an avenger,” then the soul, feeling shame, receives silence as deafness. Therefore he says, “hold your peace,” so that through the same, instruction might be born in them. Taking up my flesh for those who travel, he in a way gives them a respite. Since he himself had previously accused them as being “accusers of evils”—for they were not calling [to prayer] as they ought, but rather were stirring up grief and the...
Regarding what is being asked of him, he says: 'I take up my flesh to the teeth,' I am no longer angry against you, but against myself. Let the name of the flesh be thus smoothed over.

For often, when someone wishes to report a crushing having happened to himself, he remembers the flesh according to what is said: 'when those doing evil to me approach to eat my flesh,' (Job 2:10) instead of 'to harm me'; for it was not his flesh they were eating under the skin, but they were distressing him. Similar to this is the 'so that while living they would devour us,' which shows the aggressive action of those who force.

One might say: 'I take up my flesh to the teeth. Thus I nourish my teeth. And just as food being taken up to the teeth is thinned and its usefulness is shown, so also, nourishing my teeth and receiving the increase of benefit from the harms of these, I proceed.' But if he shows endurance through saying 'having taken up the flesh to the teeth' instead of 'not caring for the harm,' consider this.

I will place my soul in hand, if the powerful one should strike me, since he has also lifted [the hand]. In agreement with the 'having taken up my flesh to the teeth,' one should also strike upon the 'I will place my soul in hand,' so that he is saying: 'and I also despise my own soul, being subject to the one striking me and having already been subjected to this, in order to benefit you in some way,' thereby declaring the God who has consented with the one asking him. 'I am therefore ready to be given over to death.'

But if he says this regarding the change that is about to be, it is worthy of the one understanding to observe: 'since he has also lifted' does not contradict, calling God good because he rescues from those who afflict; 'I will indeed speak and convict against him,' and this will result for me in salvation. In all things, his zeal is to instruct the friends concerning the cause of the oppressors, so that he might win them over not to think against him.

For he reckoned this as salvation, to know this and the account of the providence concerning this, which he wished to make manifest by saying 'and I will convict'; for often the conviction signifies the proof, just as Paul says: 'all things being convicted are made manifest by the light,' (Eph 5:13) and again 'faith is of the things hoped for.' (Heb 11:1)
